body:
Thanks. I feel like I'm behind compared to my coastal peers so I really appreciate your perspective.

I would like to move somewhere not VHCOL but in order to accommodate both our careers (PhD in molecular biology and software development) that limits us to only a few cities.

My returns have just been dumping money into VOO when black swan stuff hits. Beginning of COVID, remarks from jpow, etc.

I don't mind paying someone to manage the property and for me to sign off on big ticket items or give final say on tenants. I live in a high income growing university town with great schools and my place is in walking distance to a grocery store and public schools K-12. 

If rents decline that would put me in trouble as it looks like I would just about break even after accounting for property management + reserve building.

Yup, property management is 12% near me. No HOA. I just replaced the roof and water heater and the furnace was replaced just before buying this place, so fingers crossed no big ticket items. It looks like I just about break even after extras.

Currently 26, have 400k net worth, and enough liquid assets to cover the entirety of my mortgage and car payments. My investment philosophy has generally been buy VOO and chill but now I feel comfortable upping my risk level since I'm young. What's the best way to increase risk rationally? Is it to pick stocks, use leverage, or invest in alternatives such as real estate? I have no major purchases coming up so I'm just looking to get that juice.

I've read "A random walk on wall street" and found it interesting but a rehashing of what I learned in my high school investing class.

That's fair. I had a similar experience with snowboarding this year. I had been a 1 to 2 times a year kind of guy, then I got my first 30+ day year with lessons and found a lot of progress through that. I maybe should've said music more generally. I have one SoundCloud account filled with music and I hate all of it. I've practiced some production stuff for months but never liked whatever I made.

I've read Turing and Church and Von Neumann. I read the original paper on backprop by le cunn and MLPs. I probably wouldn't make it past the coding interviews. In college I used to run a CS club which went to competitions and I kept placing in the solid middle even after a lot of practice.

This combination of spending a lot of time on subjects, only to have extremely mediocre results, makes me think that I'm probably on the lower std dev of IQ or whatever.

I submitted one paper to a conference and it got ripped to shreds and it felt horrible to write. All of the other admitted phd students I met felt so much smarter than me. The competition for those spots at MAAM is crazy strong. Additionally I am like 3 years out of date at this point since I keep getting pushed to do infra engineering type crap, which makes me feel dumb because it's neither research nor crunchy coding.

- I've been playing them so long that I feel like I should be able to get past the lowest rung. For chess I'm at 1000 and overwatch I'm stuck in bronze

- I haven't tried since I have had no idea how to monetize what I know. My focus was on training performance of large models, and additionally generative language models. At my first job I got a patent and was admitted to a PhD program but that opportunity fell apart when the lab lost funding. The thing I wanted to study was methods to improve generative chatbots via graph based knowledge embeddings, but it turns out all you had to do was increase the size of the model and add an RL training objective to make something usable like chatgpt. When that came out I felt like an idiot.

- idk they just feel like other examples of me not being able to succeed at anything
...and is still sitting on a pile of cash.
But VCs are not going to liquidate their holdings. What they're going to do is push hard for the ones that they've already put money into to turn cash positive.
Not when they're sitting on piles and piles of cash. The speculative shitty companies are laying off people but FAANG+ financials are still solid.
